title: Surprising taxonomic position of a new deep-water xanthid crab species (Crustacea: Brachyura: Xanthidae) reveals a recent shallow-to-deep colonization event and morphological convergence in deep water
content:
Abstract
A new deep-sea xanthid crab species, Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus sp. nov., is described from the South China Sea at 100–300 m depth. Despite marked morphological differences from its congeners, the species shares with other Macromedaeus species the morphology of the orbito-antennular area and the third maxilliped, in addition to a highly similar male first gonopod. Multiple molecular datasets further support its placement within Macromedaeus, a common intertidal genus, as the sister species of Macromedaeus orientalis. Phylogenetic reconstruction of Xanthoidea based on mitogenomes indicates divergence from its intertidal sister species during the Middle Miocene, potentially linked to the Middle Miocene Climate Transition. Morphometric analyses of the carapace and ambulatory legs in Macromedaeus and three additional xanthoid clades that each include deep- and shallow-water species reveal a convergent evolutionary trend among deep-water xanthids: in comparison to shallow-water counterparts, they tend to have a narrower, smaller carapace, and proportionally slender, flatter ambulatory legs. These shifts are likely to reflect adaptations to deep-water nutritional and substrate conditions. Integrating morphological and molecular evidence from this new species reveals a recent shallow-to-deep transition, demonstrates that the extant deep-sea biota has a complex history of formation, with coexistence of ancient and young lineages, and highlights the profound influence of deep-water environments on morphology.
